title: One MoE layer on 2x RTX 3090
subtitle: How the Mojo expert layer splits one token's 10 experts between the GPUs and the CPU, and meets in pinned memory

nodes.label: Router kernel
nodes.desc: One warp per expert computes its score from the token's vector (the router weights are 5 MB in VRAM).

nodes.label: Top-k kernel
nodes.desc: Picks the 10 best experts on the GPU, computes their weights, and looks each up in the residency table: a VRAM slot (hot) or -1 (cold). Routing never goes back to the host.
nodes.notes: In llama.cpp the expert ids were copied to the host every layer so the CPU knew its share. That per-layer round trip is gone.

nodes.label: Hot experts
nodes.desc: The experts your own chat history uses most, packed in profile order into one VRAM pool per layer. One warp per weight row; dequantized in registers.
nodes.notes: Profile: 44-48% of experts serve 91-93% of your picks. Kernel: 60 us per layer for 10 experts, 61% of VRAM bandwidth.

nodes.label: Hot experts
nodes.desc: Same, for the second half of the model. The token's vector crosses between the GPUs through pinned memory (5-8 us).

nodes.label: Combine kernel
nodes.desc: Waits for the CPU only if this token had cold experts, then sums the 10 results in sorted id order. The order is fixed, so the answer is bit-identical wherever each expert ran.

nodes.label: llama.cpp
nodes.desc: Runs everything except the routed experts. At each layer's MoE it calls omx_moe(layer, x, y) in libomxmoe.so: about 60 lines of hook code.

nodes.label: Mailbox ring
nodes.desc: 16 slots of page-locked RAM that GPU kernels read and write directly. The GPU posts cold expert ids plus the token's vector, then a sequence number. The CPU answers with results and a done flag.
nodes.notes: Round trip 2 us, measured in Mojo. A ring, not one slot: the GPU can race ahead on tokens with nothing cold.

nodes.label: CPU worker pool
nodes.desc: Persistent pthreads created from Mojo. Worker 0 watches the mailbox; all 12 split the cold experts' rows and meet at atomic barriers. Same Mojo source as the GPU kernel, 32 lanes per AVX2 vector.
nodes.notes: Dispatch 1 us, versus 236 us for Mojo's parallelize(): that alone took MoE time from 47 to 36 ms per token.

nodes.label: Cold experts
nodes.desc: Every expert not pinned in VRAM, read straight from the memory-mapped GGUF. Hot experts' pages are released after their VRAM copy, so RAM holds the cold ones.

nodes.label: Model file
nodes.desc: The 4-bit model on NVMe. Experts are loaded once at start (35 GB into VRAM in about 25 s); cold experts reach RAM through the page cache.

nodes.label: Engram rows
nodes.desc: The 28.8 GB n-gram table. With -lzm on, only the rows a token needs are read, so the table no longer fills RAM.

flows.name: One token through one layer
flows.desc: About 150 us per layer, 48 layers per token.

steps.note: llama.cpp finishes attention and hands the token's vector to the Mojo layer.
The 10 winners are split: say 9 hot (in VRAM) and 1 cold (only in RAM).
The cold expert's id and the token's vector are written straight into pinned host memory.
Worker 0 sees the sequence number change and wakes all 12 workers in about a microsecond.
Meanwhile the GPU runs the 9 hot experts at once.
The CPU reads the cold expert once from RAM and computes it with the same Mojo math.
Results land in the mailbox; the done flag releases the waiting combine kernel.
All 10 are summed in a fixed order and the vector goes back to llama.cpp for the next layer.

flows.name: From 72.9 ms to 8.6 ms
flows.desc: The four fixes behind milestone 4 (MoE time per token, 48 layers).

steps.note: Bug: the first launch of each kernel loads its module and waits for an idle GPU, deadlocking against a waiting combine. Fix: launch every kernel once at start.
72.9 -> 47 ms: Mojo's parallelize() cost 236 us per call, twice per cold request.
47 -> 36 ms: persistent spinning pthreads made from Mojo; wake-up in 1 us.
Cold experts were coming off the SSD at 650 MB/s: loading hot experts had evicted them from RAM.
36 -> 8.6 ms: release hot experts' pages after their VRAM copy, so RAM keeps the cold set.

flows.name: Same bits on either device
flows.desc: Why moving an expert between GPU and CPU never changes the text.

steps.note: On the GPU, each of 32 threads in a warp owns a lane and runs a fixed chain of multiply-adds.
On the CPU, the same Mojo function runs with all 32 lanes in one SIMD vector, in the same order.
Lanes are summed by the same butterfly tree, experts in sorted id order, with our own exp() on both.
Result: 1,200 of 1,200 random tokens bit-identical, and the same greedy text with half the hot experts moved to the CPU.
